# Exhaustive Search Methods



Exhaustive search methods in SCimilarity provide complete, distance-threshold-based cell similarity searches without the approximation inherent in K-NN indexing approaches. These methods compute pairwise cosine distances between query embeddings and every cell in the reference dataset, ensuring comprehensive retrieval of all cells within a specified maximum distance threshold. While computationally more intensive than HNSW-based K-NN searches, exhaustive methods guarantee complete coverage and are ideal for targeted analyses where precision outweighs query speed constraints.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L475-L560), [cell_search_knn.py](src/scimilarity/cell_search_knn.py#L1-L70)

## Exhaustive Search Architecture

The exhaustive search architecture leverages precomputed embeddings stored in TileDB arrays, enabling efficient batch processing of large-scale cell atlases. The core design separates three computational concerns: embedding retrieval via TileDB I/O, pairwise distance computation using SciPy's optimized distance routines, and result filtering through metadata predicates and distance thresholds. This modular approach allows the system to scale to millions of cells through configurable buffering strategies while maintaining exact distance calculations.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Query Embeddings] --> B[Batched Embedding Retrieval]
    B --> C[Cosine Distance Computation]
    C --> D{Metadata Filter Present?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Apply Metadata Predicate]
    D -->|No| F{Distance ≤ max_dist?}
    E --> F
    F -->|Yes| G[Collect Hit Indices]
    F -->|No| H[Next Batch]
    G --> I{More Batches?}
    H --> I
    I -->|Yes| B
    I -->|No| J[Sort Results by Distance]
    J --> K[Annotate with Metadata]
    K --> L[Return nn_idxs, nn_dists, metadata]
    
    style A fill:#e3f2fd
    style C fill:#fff3e0
    style G fill:#e8f5e9
    style L fill:#f3e5f5
```

The batch processing pipeline iterates through precomputed embeddings in chunks determined by the `buffer_size` parameter (default: 100,000 cells), preventing memory exhaustion on large datasets while maintaining computational efficiency. Each batch retrieves embeddings via `get_precomputed_embeddings()`, computes cosine distances using `scipy.spatial.distance.cdist()`, applies optional metadata filters, and collects cells meeting the distance threshold before proceeding to the next batch.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L475-L560), [utils.py](src/scimilarity/utils.py#L733-L784)

## Core Exhaustive Search Method

The `search_exhaustive()` method implements the fundamental exhaustive search algorithm, accepting query embeddings as input and returning all cells within a specified cosine distance threshold. The method supports both single-cell queries (1D arrays reshaped to 2D) and batch queries (multi-row 2D arrays), with each row representing a distinct query that yields its own neighbor list.

**Parameters and Configuration:**

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `embeddings` | numpy.ndarray | required | Query embeddings, shape (n_queries, latent_dim) or (latent_dim,) |
| `max_dist` | float | 0.03 | Maximum cosine distance threshold for neighbor inclusion |
| `metadata_filter` | dict | None | Metadata predicates as `{column: value}` pairs |
| `buffer_size` | int | 100,000 | Number of cells processed per batch |

The metadata filtering mechanism applies logical AND across all specified column-value pairs, enabling complex filtering like `{"tissue": "lung", "disease": "healthy"}`. When multiple filter conditions are specified, cells must satisfy all conditions to be retained as hits. This filtering occurs after distance computation, ensuring spatial filtering precedes metadata filtering for optimal performance.

> [!TIP]
> Adjust `buffer_size` based on available RAM and dataset size. Smaller values (10,000-50,000) reduce memory pressure but increase I/O overhead, while larger values (200,000+) improve throughput on systems with substantial memory.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L475-L560)

## Centroid-Based Exhaustive Search

The `search_centroid_exhaustive()` method extends exhaustive search to centroid queries, where a single representative embedding is computed from a collection of cells marked in the input AnnData object. This approach is particularly useful for querying with cell type signatures, gene expression patterns, or manually curated cell populations. The method includes built-in quality control metrics to assess centroid coherence before proceeding with the search.

**Centroid Computation Process:**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Marked Cells in adata] --> B[Extract Raw Counts]
    B --> C[Compute Gene-wise Sums]
    C --> D[Log Normalize to 1e4]
    D --> E[Generate Centroid Embedding]
    E --> F[Perform Exhaustive Search]
    F --> G{QC Enabled?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Cluster Query Cells]
    H --> I[Compute Query Coherence]
    I --> J[Return Results + QC Stats]
    G -->|No| K[Return Results]
    
    style E fill:#fff9c4
    style I fill:#ffe0b2
```

The centroid is computed from raw counts using the `get_centroid()` utility function, which sums gene expression values across all marked cells and applies log1p normalization to a target sum of 10,000. This approach ensures the centroid represents the aggregate expression profile of the query population in the same space used during model training.

**Quality Control Mechanism:**

When `qc=True` (default), the method performs k-means clustering (k=10 by default) on the embeddings of all cells used to construct the centroid. For each cluster centroid, it performs a nearest neighbor search to identify overlapping cells with the exhaustive search results. The mean overlap across all clusters is reported as `query_coherence`—higher values indicate a more tightly clustered, coherent query population. Low coherence scores suggest the input cells are dispersed in embedding space, which may produce ambiguous search results.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L561-L653), [utils.py](src/scimilarity/utils.py#L304-L326)

## Cluster Centroid Exhaustive Search

The `search_cluster_centroids_exhaustive()` method provides systematic centroid-based queries for all clusters identified in a dataset, or a specific cluster of interest. This is particularly valuable for comprehensive cell type annotation workflows where you need to compare multiple cell populations against a reference atlas simultaneously.

**Method Workflow:**

1. **Cluster Identification**: Extracts cluster labels from `adata.obs[cluster_key]`, optionally filtering to a single `cluster_label`
2. **Data Alignment**: Aligns gene expression data to the model's gene order using `align_dataset()`
3. **Centroid Computation**: Computes log-normalized centroids for each cluster using `get_cluster_centroids()`
4. **Batch Embedding**: Generates embeddings for all centroids via `get_embeddings()`
5. **Exhaustive Search**: Performs exhaustive search for each centroid through `search_exhaustive()`
6. **Result Organization**: Structures results with cluster labels as dictionary keys for easy access

The `skip_null` parameter (default: True) excludes cells with null/NaN cluster labels from centroid computation, ensuring robust centroids. When processing multiple clusters, results are returned as dictionaries keyed by cluster label, enabling straightforward analysis of cell type-specific similarity patterns across studies and tissues.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L654-L744), [utils.py](src/scimilarity/utils.py#L374-L443)

## TileDB Integration and Performance Optimization

Exhaustive search methods rely on TileDB dense arrays for efficient storage and retrieval of precomputed embeddings. The `embedding_from_tiledb()` utility implements optimized I/O patterns with a default 50GB memory budget, enabling efficient slicing and multi-index queries on large-scale embedding matrices.

**Key Performance Characteristics:**

| Aspect | Implementation Detail | Performance Impact |
|--------|---------------------|-------------------|
| **Memory Budget** | 50GB default via TileDB config | Enables caching of frequently accessed regions |
| **Index Sorting** | Pre-sorts cell indices for sequential access | Maximizes TileDB's chunk-based I/O efficiency |
| **Batch Processing** | Configurable `buffer_size` parameter | Balances memory usage vs. I/O overhead |
| **Distance Metric** | SciPy's `cdist()` with cosine metric | Optimized C implementation, batch-parallel |

The indexing strategy requires sorting cell indices before TileDB queries, then unsorting results to match original order. This approach maximizes TileDB's ability to read contiguous chunks from disk, reducing seek operations and improving throughput for large-scale queries.

> [!TIP]
> For production deployments with frequent exhaustive searches, pre-warm the TileDB cache by accessing embeddings once before peak usage periods. This reduces first-query latency and ensures consistent performance.

Sources: [utils.py](src/scimilarity/utils.py#L733-L784), [build_cellsearch_knn.py](scripts/build_cellsearch_knn.py#L8-L9)

## Comparison with K-NN Search Methods

Exhaustive search methods provide fundamentally different guarantees compared to approximate K-NN search approaches, making them suitable for different analytical scenarios. Understanding these tradeoffs is essential for selecting the appropriate method for your use case.

**Method Comparison Matrix:**

| Characteristic | Exhaustive Search | K-NN Search (HNSW) |
|---------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Completeness** | 100% (all cells within threshold) | Approximate (may miss some cells) |
| **Distance Precision** | Exact cosine distances | Approximate distances |
| **Query Time** | O(n) linear with dataset size | O(log n) logarithmic with dataset size |
| **Memory Usage** | Higher (batch processing) | Lower (in-memory index) |
| **Result Size** | Variable (depends on threshold) | Fixed (k neighbors) |
| **Best Use Case** | Precision-critical analyses | Large-scale exploratory searches |

Exhaustive search is particularly valuable when you need complete coverage of similar cells, such as identifying all cells within a tight distance threshold for downstream differential expression analysis. K-NN methods, described in [K-NN Search with HNSW](10-k-nn-search-with-hnsw), are better suited for rapid prototyping and exploratory analysis where approximate results are acceptable.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L206-L276), [cell_search_knn.py](src/scimilarity/cell_search_knn.py#L64-L104)

## Practical Implementation Guide

**Basic Exhaustive Search:**

```python
from scimilarity import CellQuery

# Initialize query object
cq = CellQuery(model_path="/path/to/model")

# Get query embeddings
embeddings = cq.get_embeddings(query_counts)

# Perform exhaustive search
nn_idxs, nn_dists, metadata = cq.search_exhaustive(
    embeddings,
    max_dist=0.03,
    metadata_filter={"tissue": "lung"},
    buffer_size=100000
)
```

**Centroid-Based Search with QC:**

```python
# Mark cells for centroid construction
adata.obs["used_in_query"] = (adata.obs["cell_type"] == "macrophage").astype(int)

# Perform centroid search with quality control
centroid_emb, nn_idxs, nn_dists, metadata, qc_stats = cq.search_centroid_exhaustive(
    adata,
    centroid_key="used_in_query",
    max_dist=0.03,
    qc=True,
    qc_params={"k_clusters": 10}
)

# Evaluate query coherence
print(f"Query coherence: {qc_stats['query_coherence']:.2%}")
```

**Multi-Cluster Analysis:**

```python
# Search all clusters in a dataset
centroids, cluster_labels, nn_dict, dist_dict, all_metadata = cq.search_cluster_centroids_exhaustive(
    adata,
    cluster_key="leiden",
    max_dist=0.035,
    buffer_size=150000
)

# Access results for specific clusters
for cluster in cluster_labels:
    cluster_hits = len(nn_dict[cluster][0])
    print(f"{cluster}: {cluster_hits} similar cells found")
```


# Metadata Filtering and Query Optimization



Metadata filtering and query optimization in scimilarity enables precise cell search operations by constraining results based on biological and experimental attributes while maintaining computational efficiency through strategic buffer management and distance-based pruning.

## Metadata Filtering Architecture

The metadata filtering system operates on a dictionary-based query model where keys represent metadata column names and values specify valid terms for filtering. This design allows for flexible, multi-criteria filtering across biological dimensions such as tissue type, disease state, study origin, and sample identifiers. The filtering occurs during exhaustive search operations, where each batch of cells undergoes both distance-based similarity evaluation and metadata attribute validation before being included in the result set.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L479-L482), [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L521-L532)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Query Embeddings] --> B{Exhaustive Search}
    B --> C[Batch Processing<br/>buffer_size: 100,000]
    C --> D[Distance Computation<br/>cdist cosine metric]
    D --> E{max_dist Filter}
    E -->|Pass| F[Metadata Filter Application]
    E -->|Fail| G[Discard Results]
    F --> H{metadata_filter<br/>Dictionary}
    H -->|Multiple Keys| I[Logical AND<br/>np.all metadata_hits]
    H -->|Single Key| J[Direct Equality Check]
    I --> K[Combine with Distance Hits<br/>np.vstack[hits, metadata_hits]]
    J --> K
    K --> L[Sort by Distance<br/>np.argsort]
    L --> M[Return Filtered Results<br/>nn_idxs, nn_dists, metadata]
```

> [!TIP]
> The metadata filtering logic applies logical AND operations when multiple filter keys are specified, ensuring results satisfy all specified constraints simultaneously. This is implemented through `np.all(np.vstack(metadata_hits), axis=0)` which combines multiple boolean condition arrays.

## Metadata Schema and Storage

Cell metadata is persisted in TileDB format with a standardized schema containing core biological and experimental attributes. The `CellQuery` class initializes by loading this metadata into memory through the `metadata_tiledb_uri` parameter (default: "cell_metadata"), which provides rapid access during search operations. The metadata structure includes essential columns such as study, sample, tissue, disease, data_type (train/test/NA), and prediction fields derived from cell ontology mappings.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L36-L37), [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L77-L85), [build_cellsearch_metadata.py](scripts/build_cellsearch_metadata.py#L60-L63), [build_cellsearch_metadata.py](scripts/build_cellsearch_metadata.py#L65-L69)

The metadata construction process, implemented in `build_cellsearch_metadata.py`, performs several critical transformations including column renaming (datasetID→study, sampleID→sample, etc.), cell ontology ID to name mapping, and prediction enrichment through KNN-based annotation models. The resulting schema provides a comprehensive view of each cell's provenance and biological classification.

| Metadata Column | Source/Transform | Description | Example Values |
|----------------|------------------|-------------|----------------|
| study | datasetID column | Research study identifier | "GSE123456" |
| sample | sampleID column | Biological sample identifier | "S1", "Tumor_01" |
| tissue | tissue column | Tissue type annotation | "lung", "brain" |
| disease | disease column | Disease state annotation | "normal", "cancer" |
| data_type | train/val indices | Partition membership | "train", "test", "NA" |
| prediction | KNN annotation | Predicted cell type | "macrophage", "T cell" |
| prediction_nn_dist | KNN distances | Annotation confidence metric | 0.015, 0.023 |
| author_label | cellTypeOntologyID mapping | Original cell type label | "CL0000084" |

## Exhaustive Search with Metadata Filtering

The `search_exhaustive` method implements the primary metadata filtering interface, combining distance-based similarity search with attribute-based constraints. This method processes cells in configurable buffer batches (default: 100,000 cells) to balance memory usage with computational throughput, making it suitable for large-scale cell atlases containing millions of cells.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L475-L560)

The search workflow begins by computing pairwise cosine distances between query embeddings and batches of precomputed cell embeddings using scipy's `cdist` function. For each cell in the query batch, the method first applies a distance threshold filter using `max_dist` (default: 0.03), then overlays the metadata filter when specified. The metadata filtering logic creates boolean hit arrays for each key-value pair in the `metadata_filter` dictionary and combines them with the distance-based hits using logical AND operations.

```python
# Distance filtering
hits = nn_dist[row] <= max_dist

# Metadata filtering
if metadata_filter is not None:
    metadata_hits = []
    for k, v in metadata_filter.items():
        metadata_hits.append(
            (self.cell_metadata.loc[nn_idx, k] == v).values
        )
    if len(metadata_hits) > 1:
        metadata_hits = np.all(np.vstack(metadata_hits), axis=0)
    hits = np.all(np.vstack([hits, metadata_hits]), axis=0)
```

This implementation ensures that only cells satisfying both similarity criteria (within max_dist) and metadata constraints (matching all specified key-value pairs) are included in the results. The final results are sorted by increasing distance before being returned.

> [!TIP]
> For optimal query performance, apply the most restrictive metadata filters first and use distance thresholds that match your application's precision requirements. The default max_dist of 0.03 provides a balance between specificity and recall, but can be adjusted based on downstream analysis needs.

## Centroid-Based Query Filtering

Centroid-based search methods extend metadata filtering capabilities to support queries derived from cell groups or clusters. The `search_centroid_exhaustive` method accepts an AnnData object with a binary marker column (`centroid_key`) identifying cells to include in the centroid calculation. This enables queries representing biological conditions, disease states, or experimental treatments while maintaining the same metadata filtering interface as standard cell queries.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L561-L653)

The centroid computation uses the `get_centroid` utility function operating on the counts layer of the input AnnData object, followed by embedding generation through the trained model. The resulting centroid embedding is then passed to the standard `search_exhaustive` method with the same `max_dist`, `metadata_filter`, and `buffer_size` parameters. This architecture ensures consistent filtering behavior across single-cell and group-based queries.

The method optionally performs quality control (QC) through k-means clustering of the query cells and coherence assessment against the search results. The QC statistics include a `query_coherence` metric measuring the overlap between cluster centroids' nearest neighbors and the query results, providing insight into the internal consistency of the query cell population.

## Cluster-Based Query Filtering

For applications requiring queries across multiple cell types or conditions, the `search_cluster_centroids_exhaustive` method provides a comprehensive interface for filtering at the cluster level. This method accepts an AnnData object with cluster labels specified through `cluster_key` and optionally restricts analysis to a specific `cluster_label`.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L654-L744)

Cluster centroids are computed using the `get_cluster_centroids` utility function, which performs gene ordering alignment and handles null/NaN cluster labels based on the `skip_null` parameter. Each centroid embedding is then searched exhaustively against the reference database with consistent metadata filtering applied across all centroids. The results are organized as dictionaries keyed by cluster labels, enabling efficient post-query analysis at the cluster level.

The method adds a `centroid` column to the returned metadata DataFrame, mapping each result to its originating cluster through the `embedding_idx` field. This structure supports downstream analyses such as cluster-specific annotation validation or comparative studies across cell type distributions.

## Sample-Level Metadata Aggregation

Beyond cell-level filtering, the `compile_sample_metadata` method provides sample-level aggregation of nearest neighbor results. This function operates on the indices returned from search operations and aggregates counts by specified hierarchical levels (default: ["study", "sample", "tissue", "disease"]) to enable quantitative comparisons across studies and experimental conditions.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L150-L205)

The aggregation computes both absolute cell counts and fractional representation for each study-sample combination. The fraction calculation uses the total cell count per study-sample pair from the full metadata database, providing normalized measures that account for varying sample sizes across studies. This output is particularly valuable for identifying enriched cell types in specific biological conditions or assessing the generalizability of query results across different experimental batches.

```python
study_sample_cells = self.cell_metadata.groupby(
    ["study", "sample"], observed=True
).size()

for i, row in df.iterrows():
    total_cells = study_sample_cells.loc[(row["study"], row["sample"])]
    fraction.append(row["cells"] / total_cells)
    total.append(total_cells)
df["fraction"] = fraction
df["total"] = total
```

## Performance Optimization Strategies

Query optimization in scimilarity leverages multiple strategies to balance computational efficiency with result quality. The buffer_size parameter controls batch processing granularity, with the default of 100,000 cells representing a practical compromise between memory usage and I/O efficiency. For systems with abundant memory, increasing buffer_size can reduce iteration overhead, while memory-constrained environments may require smaller values to prevent out-of-memory conditions.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L479-L482), [build_cellsearch_metadata.py](scripts/build_cellsearch_metadata.py#L17)

The precomputed embeddings stored in TileDB enable rapid retrieval without re-encoding, and the indexed metadata structure supports efficient subset extraction. The distance threshold (max_dist) provides an early filtering mechanism that eliminates dissimilar cells before metadata filtering is applied, reducing unnecessary boolean operations on metadata attributes.

> [!TIP]
> When working with very large cell atlases (>10 million cells), consider partitioning queries by tissue or study using metadata filters to limit the search space. The TileDB-based storage system supports efficient columnar reads, making it well-suited for this filtering pattern.

## Query Method Comparison

The following table summarizes the metadata filtering capabilities across different query methods in the CellQuery class:

| Method | Input Type | Use Case | Metadata Filter Support | Output Structure |
|--------|-----------|----------|------------------------|------------------|
| search_exhaustive | Embeddings | Single/multiple cell queries | Full dictionary filter | List of arrays per query |
| search_centroid_exhaustive | AnnData + centroid_key | Group-based centroid queries | Full dictionary filter | Single centroid results |
| search_cluster_centroids_exhaustive | AnnData + cluster_key | Multi-cluster comparison | Full dictionary filter | Dictionary keyed by cluster |

All three methods share the same underlying `search_exhaustive` implementation, ensuring consistent filtering behavior and parameter semantics. The choice of method depends primarily on the query structure rather than the filtering requirements.

## Advanced Filtering Patterns

Complex biological queries can be constructed through combinations of metadata filters and distance thresholds. For example, identifying macrophages specifically from lung tissue in normal samples would use:

```python
metadata_filter = {
    "tissue": "lung",
    "disease": "normal",
    "prediction": "macrophage"
}
nn_idxs, nn_dists, metadata = cq.search_exhaustive(
    embeddings,
    max_dist=0.03,
    metadata_filter=metadata_filter,
    buffer_size=100000
)
```

For progressive refinement, queries can be executed with relaxed constraints initially, followed by subsequent filtering on the returned metadata DataFrame. This pattern is particularly useful when the exact cell type names are uncertain or when exploring related biological states.

Sources: [cell_query.py](src/scimilarity/cell_query.py#L544-L549)

## Next Steps

For comprehensive understanding of the search infrastructure, review [K-NN Search with HNSW](10-k-nn-search-with-hnsw) for approximate search methods and [Exhaustive Search Methods](11-exhaustive-search-methods) for additional distance computation strategies. The [Cell Query API Reference](9-cell-query-api-reference) provides complete parameter documentation for all query methods.

# Cell Annotation API Reference



The Cell Annotation API provides automated cell type classification through similarity-based inference in latent space. By leveraging pre-trained embeddings and k-nearest neighbor search, this module enables high-throughput annotation of single-cell transcriptomics data with configurable filtering and prediction weighting strategies. The API is built on top of the CellSearchKNN infrastructure [cell_annotation.py#L6-L320](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L6-L320) and integrates seamlessly with AnnData workflows for end-to-end analysis pipelines.

## Core Architecture

CellAnnotation extends CellSearchKNN, inheriting embedding generation and k-NN search capabilities while adding specialized functionality for cell type prediction and reference dataset filtering. The class loads a pre-trained model along with a reference k-NN index containing labeled cell types, enabling rapid classification of query cells by their nearest neighbors in the embedding space [cell_annotation.py#L6-L50](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L6-L50).

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class CellEmbedding {
        +get_embeddings(data)
        +gene_order: list
    }
    
    class CellSearchKNN {
        +load_knn_index(knn_file)
        +get_nearest_neighbors(embeddings, k, ef)
    }
    
    class CellAnnotation {
        +classes: set
        +safelist: set
        +blocklist: set
        +idx2label: dict
        +idx2study: dict
        +get_predictions_knn(embeddings, k, ef, weighting)
        +safelist_celltypes(labels)
        +blocklist_celltypes(labels)
        +reset_knn()
        +annotate_dataset(data)
    }
    
    CellEmbedding <|-- CellSearchKNN
    CellSearchKNN <|-- CellAnnotation
```

The annotation system requires three key files at initialization: the trained model weights, the labeled k-NN index in HNSW format, and a reference labels TSV file mapping indices to cell type names [cell_annotation.py#L23-L50](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L23-L50). The `filenames` parameter supports custom file paths for flexibility in different deployment scenarios.

## Class Initialization

### Constructor Parameters

```python
CellAnnotation(model_path, use_gpu=False, filenames=None)
```

The CellAnnotation constructor initializes the annotation system by loading the neural network model and reference k-NN index from the specified model directory [cell_annotation.py#L23-L50](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L23-L50).

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `model_path` | str | required | Path to directory containing model files (model weights, k-NN index, reference labels) |
| `use_gpu` | bool | False | Enable GPU acceleration for embedding computation |
| `filenames` | dict | None | Custom filename mappings for 'knn' and 'celltype_labels' files |

The constructor automatically creates an annotation subdirectory within `model_path` and establishes file paths for the k-NN index (`labelled_kNN.bin`) and reference labels (`reference_labels.tsv`) [cell_annotation.py#L32-L45](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L32-L45). The reference labels file is parsed to build `idx2label` and `idx2study` mappings that associate k-NN indices with cell type names and study origins.

## Cell Type Filtering

### Blocklist Cell Types

```python
blocklist_celltypes(labels)
```

The blocklist mechanism prevents certain cell types from being considered during annotation by marking corresponding k-NN indices as deleted [cell_annotation.py#L92-L116](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L92-L116). This is useful when you want to exclude broad or redundant categories (e.g., "T cell" when you only want specific T cell subtypes).

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `labels` | List[str] or Set[str] | Cell type labels to exclude from predictions |

> [!TIP]
> Blocklists and safelists are mutually exclusive. Setting a blocklist automatically clears any existing safelist, and vice versa. The filter persists for the lifetime of the CellAnnotation instance until explicitly reset.

### Safelist Cell Types

```python
safelist_celltypes(labels)
```

Safelisting restricts predictions to only the specified cell types by marking all k-NN indices as deleted and then unmarking only the safelisted categories [cell_annotation.py#L118-L146](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L118-L146). This approach reduces annotation noise and classification conflicts, particularly useful when analyzing tissues with known cell type compositions.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `labels` | List[str] or Set[str] | Cell type labels to allow in predictions |

### Reset K-NN Filters

```python
reset_knn()
```

The reset method clears all blocklist and safelist filters by unmarking all deleted k-NN indices [cell_annotation.py#L74-L89](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L74-L89). This restores the full reference dataset for subsequent predictions, useful when switching between different annotation strategies.

## Prediction Methods

### Get Predictions K-NN

```python
get_predictions_knn(embeddings, k=50, ef=100, weighting=False, disable_progress=False)
```

This core method performs cell type prediction by finding nearest neighbors for query embeddings and computing consensus labels through majority voting or distance-weighted voting [cell_annotation.py#L148-L279](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L148-L279). The method returns comprehensive prediction statistics for downstream analysis.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `embeddings` | numpy.ndarray | required | Cell embeddings from the pre-trained model |
| `k` | int | 50 | Number of nearest neighbors to query |
| `ef` | int | 100 | Size of dynamic candidate list for HNSW search (higher = better accuracy, slower) |
| `weighting` | bool | False | Enable distance-weighted voting (closer neighbors get more influence) |
| `disable_progress` | bool | False | Hide tqdm progress bar |

> [!TIP]
> The `ef` parameter controls the search-time quality/speed tradeoff. For production deployments, start with `ef=100`. For critical applications requiring maximum precision, increase to `ef=200-500`. For rapid prototyping, decrease to `ef=50`.

**Return Values**

The method returns a tuple of four values:
- `predictions`: pandas.Series with predicted cell type labels for each query cell
- `nn_idxs`: 2D numpy array [num_cells × k] containing indices of nearest neighbors
- `nn_dists`: 2D numpy array [num_cells × k] containing distances to nearest neighbors
- `stats`: pandas.DataFrame with detailed prediction metrics

The statistics DataFrame includes the following columns:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `hits` | JSON string of cell type counts among k neighbors |
| `hits_weighted` | JSON string of distance-weighted cell type counts |
| `min_dist` | Minimum distance to any neighbor |
| `max_dist` | Maximum distance among k neighbors |
| `vs2nd` | Ratio of best hit count to sum of best + second best hits |
| `vsAll` | Ratio of best hit count to sum of all hits |
| `vs2nd_weighted` | Distance-weighted version of `vs2nd` |
| `vsAll_weighted` | Distance-weighted version of `vsAll` |

These metrics enable confidence scoring and quality filtering of predictions. High `vs2nd` values (e.g., >0.8) indicate unambiguous predictions, while low values suggest ambiguous classifications that may require manual review.

### Annotate Dataset

```python
annotate_dataset(data)
```

The `annotate_dataset` method provides a high-level interface for complete dataset annotation, handling embedding generation, alignment, and prediction statistics in a single call [cell_annotation.py#L281-L320](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L281-L320). The method assumes input data has been log-normalized and automatically aligns the gene order to match the model's training data.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `data` | anndata.AnnData | AnnData object with log-normalized expression matrix |

**Modifications to AnnData Object**

The method enriches the input AnnData object with several new fields:

| Field | Location | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `X_scimilarity` | `data.obsm` | Cell embeddings from the SCimilarity model |
| `celltype_hint` | `data.obs` | Predicted cell type labels |
| `min_dist` | `data.obs` | Minimum distance to nearest neighbors |
| `celltype_hits` | `data.obs` | JSON string of neighbor cell type counts |
| `celltype_hits_weighted` | `data.obs` | JSON string of weighted neighbor counts |
| `celltype_hint_stat` | `data.obs` | Confidence score (vsAll metric) |
| `celltype_hint_weighted_stat` | `data.obs` | Weighted confidence score |

## Properties

### Classes Property

```python
classes
```

The `classes` property returns the complete set of viable prediction classes available in the reference dataset [cell_annotation.py#L68-L71](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L68-L71). This read-only property is useful for inspecting the available cell types before configuring safelists or blocklists.

```python
>>> ca = CellAnnotation(model_path="/opt/data/model")
>>> print(f"Available classes: {len(ca.classes)}")
Available classes: 237
```

## Usage Workflow

The typical workflow for cell annotation involves initialization, optional filtering, prediction, and downstream analysis. The following diagram illustrates the complete process:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Load Data<br/>AnnData object] --> B[Preprocess<br/>align_dataset + lognorm_counts]
    B --> C[Initialize CellAnnotation<br/>load model and k-NN index]
    C --> D{Apply Filtering?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Set safelist or blocklist<br/>restrict prediction classes]
    D -->|No| F[Get predictions<br/>get_predictions_knn or annotate_dataset]
    E --> F
    F --> G[Analyze predictions<br/>confidence scores, statistics]
    G --> H{Quality filter?}
    H -->|Yes| I[Filter cells by confidence metrics]
    H -->|No| J[Visualize and interpret<br/>UMAP, feature plots]
    I --> J
```

## Example Usage

### Basic Annotation Pipeline

```python
from scimilarity import CellAnnotation
from scimilarity.utils import align_dataset, lognorm_counts
import scanpy as sc

# Load data
data = sc.read("your_data.h5ad")

# Initialize annotation
ca = CellAnnotation(model_path="/opt/data/model")

# Preprocess data to match model requirements
data = align_dataset(data, ca.gene_order)
data = lognorm_counts(data)

# Annotate dataset
data = ca.annotate_dataset(data)

# Examine results
print(data.obs["celltype_hint"].value_counts())
```

### Constrained Annotation with Safelist

```python
# Define cell types of interest for lung tissue analysis
lung_celltypes = [
    "type I pneumocyte",
    "type II pneumocyte", 
    "alveolar macrophage",
    "endothelial cell of lymphatic vessel",
    "lung endothelial cell",
]

# Apply safelist filter
ca.safelist_celltypes(lung_celltypes)

# Get predictions with confidence filtering
embeddings = ca.get_embeddings(data.X)
predictions, nn_idxs, nn_dists, stats = ca.get_predictions_knn(
    embeddings, 
    k=50, 
    weighting=True
)

# Filter high-confidence predictions
high_conf_mask = stats["vsAll"] > 0.8
print(f"High-confidence predictions: {high_conf_mask.sum()}/{len(predictions)}")
```

### Blocklist-Based Filtering

```python
# Exclude broad categories to prevent generic predictions
ca.blocklist_celltypes([
    "T cell",
    "B cell",
    "myeloid cell",
    "epithelial cell",
])

# Predict only specific subtypes
predictions, _, _, stats = ca.get_predictions_knn(
    embeddings,
    k=50,
    weighting=True
)
```

> [!TIP]
> When working with novel cell types not in the reference, the nearest neighbor distances (`nn_dists`) provide a useful signal. Large minimum distances indicate that the cell may represent a novel state rather than a well-characterized type. Consider visualizing `data.obs["min_dist"]` on UMAP plots to identify ambiguous or novel populations.

## Performance Considerations

The CellAnnotation class is optimized for high-throughput annotation with several performance characteristics:

- **K-NN Search Speed**: Uses HNSWlib for efficient approximate nearest neighbor search with O(log n) query complexity
- **Memory Requirements**: K-NN index typically requires 50-100 MB of RAM (configurable via `memory_budget` in `load_knn_index`)
- **GPU Acceleration**: Enable `use_gpu=True` for embedding generation on compatible hardware, providing 3-5x speedup for large datasets
- **Batch Processing**: The `get_predictions_knn` method processes all embeddings in a single batch for optimal throughput

## Integration with Other SCimilarity Modules

CellAnnotation is part of the broader SCimilarity ecosystem and integrates with several complementary modules:

- **CellEmbedding**: Provides the underlying neural network encoder for generating latent representations [cell_embedding.py](src/scimilarity/cell_embedding.py)
- **CellSearchKNN**: Inherits k-NN search infrastructure for fast neighbor queries [cell_search_knn.py](src/scimilarity/cell_search_knn.py)
- **Utils**: Provides `align_dataset` and `lognorm_counts` functions for data preprocessing [utils.py](src/scimilarity/utils.py)
- **Ontologies**: Can reference Cell Ontology terms for standardized cell type naming [ontologies.py](src/scimilarity/ontologies.py)

For detailed understanding of the underlying cell search mechanisms and K-NN optimization, see [K-NN Search with HNSW](10-k-nn-search-with-hnsw). For advanced filtering strategies and interpretation of prediction statistics, refer to [Understanding Cell Type Classification](14-understanding-cell-type-classification) and [Safelist and Blocklist Cell Types](15-safelist-and-blocklist-cell-types).

# Understanding Cell Type Classification



Cell type classification in scimilarity leverages a sophisticated k-nearest neighbors (KNN) approach operating in a learned embedding space. The system transforms high-dimensional gene expression data into compact latent representations through a trained encoder, then performs similarity search against a reference database of pre-annotated cells to generate type predictions based on consensus voting among nearest neighbors. This architecture enables rapid, scalable cell annotation across diverse biological contexts.

## Classification Architecture

The classification pipeline follows a three-stage process that transforms raw gene expression into confident cell type assignments. First, the encoder neural network projects input gene expression vectors into a 128-dimensional latent space optimized for semantic similarity between cells of the same type. Second, a hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW) index enables efficient approximate nearest neighbor search across potentially millions of reference cells. Finally, a weighted consensus mechanism aggregates predictions from the k nearest neighbors to produce final cell type labels with associated confidence metrics.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Input Gene Expression] --> B[Gene Alignment]
    B --> C[Encoder Network]
    C --> D[Latent Embedding]
    D --> E[HNSW k-NN Search]
    E --> F[Nearest Neighbors]
    F --> G[Consensus Voting]
    G --> H[Cell Type Prediction]
    G --> I[Confidence Metrics]
```

The `CellAnnotation` class orchestrates this workflow, inheriting embedding capabilities from `CellEmbedding` and k-nearest neighbor search functionality from `CellSearchKNN` [cell_annotation.py#L6](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L6-L7). During initialization, the class loads a pre-trained encoder model and a pre-built k-NN index containing reference cells with known cell type labels [cell_annotation.py#L23-L65](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L23-L65). The reference labels are stored in a TSV file mapping each index position to a cell type, with optional study metadata [cell_annotation.py#L52-L60](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L52-L60).

## KNN-Based Prediction Mechanism

The core prediction logic resides in the `get_predictions_knn` method, which retrieves k nearest neighbors for query embeddings and computes consensus predictions [cell_annotation.py#L148-L280](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L148-L280). The method supports two prediction modes: simple majority voting and distance-weighted voting controlled by the `weighting` parameter [cell_annotation.py#L210-L219](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L210-L219).

For each query cell, the system maintains two dictionaries: `celltype` counting raw occurrences and `celltype_weighted` accumulating inverse distance weights [cell_annotation.py#L201-L207](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L201-L207). When weighting is enabled, each neighbor's contribution is scaled by 1/distance, giving greater influence to more similar reference cells. The final prediction selects the cell type with maximum count or weighted count [cell_annotation.py#L211-L218](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L211-L218).

| Parameter | Default | Purpose | Impact |
|-----------|---------|---------|--------|
| `k` | 50 | Number of neighbors to retrieve | Larger values increase robustness but may dilute specificity |
| `ef` | 100 | HNSW search list size | Higher values improve recall at computational cost |
| `weighting` | False | Enable distance weighting | True gives preference to closer neighbors |

The HNSW index provides extremely fast approximate nearest neighbor search, with the `ef` parameter controlling the search quality-speed tradeoff [cell_search_knn.py#L64-L104](src/scimilarity/cell_search_knn.py#L64-L104). Setting `ef` higher than `k` typically improves accuracy by exploring a larger candidate set during traversal.

## Prediction Statistics and Confidence Metrics

Beyond simple predictions, the system computes comprehensive statistics quantifying classification confidence. The `stats` DataFrame returned by `get_predictions_knn` contains metrics that help assess prediction reliability [cell_annotation.py#L174-L193](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L174-L193):

- **hits**: JSON string with raw count for every cell type among k neighbors
- **hits_weighted**: JSON string with distance-weighted counts for each type
- **min_dist**: Minimum distance among k neighbors
- **max_dist**: Maximum distance among k neighbors
- **vs2nd**: Ratio of best count to sum of best and second-best counts
- **vsAll**: Ratio of best count to sum of all counts
- **vs2nd_weighted**: Weighted version of vs2nd
- **vsAll_weighted**: Weighted version of vsAll

The vs2nd metric measures dominance of the predicted type over the runner-up, while vsAll indicates relative strength compared to all alternatives. Values approaching 1.0 indicate high confidence, while lower values suggest ambiguous assignments. These metrics are computed for both unweighted and weighted versions to provide complementary perspectives [cell_annotation.py#L220-L240](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L220-L240).

> [!TIP]
> When analyzing vs2nd and vsAll metrics, consider a threshold of 0.7-0.8 as a reasonable indicator of high-confidence predictions, but validate this threshold for your specific biological context as the optimal value can vary by cell type diversity and reference database composition.

## Cell Type Filtering with Safelists and Blocklists

Scimilarity provides sophisticated control over the prediction space through safelist and blocklist mechanisms. These filters operate by marking specific cell type entries as deleted in the HNSW index, effectively removing them from consideration during neighbor search [cell_annotation.py#L92-L147](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L92-L147).

The `blocklist_celltypes` method excludes specified cell types from prediction, useful when you want to ignore known problematic or irrelevant categories [cell_annotation.py#L92-L107](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L92-L107). Conversely, `safelist_celltypes` restricts predictions to only specified types, implementing a conservative approach to classification [cell_annotation.py#L118-L147](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L118-L147). These operations are mutually exclusive—setting one clears the other—and persist for the lifetime of the class instance.

The filtering mechanism works by calling HNSW's `mark_deleted` and `unmark_deleted` methods, which efficiently remove or restore entries without index reconstruction [cell_annotation.py#L103-L105](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L103-L105), [cell_annotation.py#L141-L145](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L141-L145). This design enables rapid experimentation with different prediction scopes without computational overhead. The `reset_knn` method clears all filters, restoring the full prediction space [cell_annotation.py#L74-L90](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L74-L90).

## Dataset Annotation Workflow

For batch processing of single-cell datasets, the `annotate_dataset` method provides a streamlined workflow that handles the entire annotation pipeline from raw data to enriched results [cell_annotation.py#L281-L320](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L281-L320). This method accepts an AnnData object containing log-normalized gene expression and returns an annotated version with multiple useful fields.

The workflow begins by aligning the input dataset's gene order to match the encoder's expected format using the `align_dataset` utility function [cell_annotation.py#L298](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L298). After computing embeddings via the encoder, the method calls `get_predictions_knn` and stores results in the AnnData object:

- **obs["celltype_hint"]**: Predicted cell type labels
- **obs["X_scimilarity"]**: 128-dimensional latent embeddings
- **obs["min_dist"]**: Minimum neighbor distance for each cell
- **obs["celltype_hits"]**: JSON string of neighbor type counts
- **obs["celltype_hits_weighted"]**: Weighted neighbor type counts
- **obs["celltype_hint_stat"]**: vsAll confidence metric
- **obs["celltype_hint_weighted_stat"]**: Weighted vsAll confidence metric

> [!TIP]
> The embedding vectors stored in `X_scimilarity` can be used for downstream analyses such as UMAP visualization, clustering, or quality control—leverage these representations to understand how your data relates to the reference database structure.

This comprehensive annotation enables both immediate cell type assignment and retrospective analysis of prediction quality across the entire dataset.

## Relationship to Other Components

Cell type classification integrates closely with several other scimilarity systems. The encoder architecture used for projection is detailed in [Encoder and Decoder Architecture](7-encoder-and-decoder-architecture), while the underlying latent space properties are explained in [Understanding Latent Space Representations](8-understanding-latent-space-representations). The search mechanisms that power neighbor retrieval are covered in [K-NN Search with HNSW](10-k-nn-search-with-hnsw).

For advanced prediction control, [Safelist and Blocklist Cell Types](15-safelist-and-blocklist-cell-types) provides deeper exploration of filtering strategies, while [Prediction Weighting Strategies](16-prediction-weighting-strategies) offers guidance on selecting appropriate weighting schemes for different biological scenarios. These specialized topics build upon the foundational understanding presented here.

The practical application of these concepts is demonstrated in the [Cell Annotation Tutorial](tutorials), which walks through end-to-end annotation workflows with real data examples.

# Safelist and Blocklist Cell Types



Cell type filtering in SCimilarity provides precise control over the annotation search space by enabling selective inclusion (safelist) or exclusion (blocklist) of cell types from the reference database. This mechanism allows researchers to constrain predictions to biologically relevant cell type subsets, reducing annotation noise and improving specificity for focused analyses.

## Architectural Foundation

The safelist and blocklist functionality is built upon the HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) k-nearest neighbor index architecture. The `CellAnnotation` class inherits filtering capabilities from `CellSearchKNN`, which manages the kNN index structure and cell type label mappings. When a safelist or blocklist is applied, the system manipulates the deletion status of nodes within the HNSW index rather than reconstructing the index, providing efficient runtime filtering.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class CellEmbedding {
        +model
        +gene_order
        +get_embeddings()
    }
    
    class CellSearchKNN {
        -knn: HNSWIndex
        -safelist: Set
        -blocklist: Set
        -idx2label: Dict
        -label2int: Dict
        +load_knn_index()
        +get_nearest_neighbors()
        +reset_knn()
    }
    
    class CellAnnotation {
        +blocklist_celltypes(labels)
        +safelist_celltypes(labels)
        +get_predictions_knn()
        +annotate_dataset()
        +classes: Set
    }
    
    CellEmbedding <|-- CellSearchKNN
    CellSearchKNN <|-- CellAnnotation
```

The inheritance hierarchy places safelist/blocklist functionality in `CellSearchKNN` where the kNN index resides, while `CellAnnotation` provides domain-specific methods for applying these filters during cell type annotation workflows. The `idx2label` and `label2int` dictionaries maintain bidirectional mappings between integer indices in the kNN index and human-readable cell type labels.

Sources: [cell_search_knn.py](src/scimilarity/cell_search_knn.py#L1-L39), [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L1-L30)

## Blocklist Mechanism

The blocklist operation explicitly removes specified cell types from consideration during k-nearest neighbor search. When you invoke `blocklist_celltypes()`, the system first resets the kNN index to clear any existing filters, then marks all reference cells belonging to the specified labels as deleted within the HNSW structure.

```python
def blocklist_celltypes(self, labels: Union[List[str], Set[str]]):
    """Blocklist celltypes.
    
    Blocking a celltype will persist for this instance of the class and 
    subsequent predictions will have this blocklist. Blocklists and 
    safelists are mutually exclusive, setting one will clear the other.
    """
    self.reset_knn()  # Clear previous state
    self.blocklist = set(labels)
    self.safelist = None  # Ensure mutual exclusivity
    
    for i, celltype_name in self.idx2label.items():
        if celltype_name in self.blocklist:
            self.knn.mark_deleted(i)  # Mark blocklist cells as deleted
```

The implementation iterates through all cells in the reference, checking each against the blocklist set. When a match is found, the cell's index is marked as deleted using the HNSW library's `mark_deleted()` method. This prevents those cells from being returned in subsequent nearest neighbor queries, effectively filtering them out without modifying the underlying index structure.

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L92-L117)

## Safelist Mechanism

The safelist operation takes an inclusionary approach, explicitly permitting only specified cell types to appear in annotation results. The implementation uses a "mark all, then unmark permitted" strategy: it first marks every cell in the reference as deleted, then selectively unmarks only those cells belonging to safelisted cell types.

```python
def safelist_celltypes(self, labels: Union[List[str], Set[str]]):
    """Safelist celltypes.
    
    Safelisting a celltype will persist for this instance of the class and 
    subsequent predictions will have this safelist. Blocklists and safelists 
    are mutually exclusive, setting one will clear the other.
    """
    self.blocklist = None  # Ensure mutual exclusivity
    self.safelist = set(labels)
    
    # Mark all cells as deleted first
    for i in self.idx2label:
        try:
            self.knn.mark_deleted(i)
        except:
            pass  # Ignore exceptions if already marked
    
    # Unmark only safelisted cell types
    for i, celltype_name in self.idx2label.items():
        if celltype_name in self.safelist:
            self.knn.unmark_deleted(i)  # Restore access to safelisted cells
```

This approach ensures that only explicitly permitted cell types can appear in results. The try-except block handles the case where a cell might already be marked as deleted, which can occur if the kNN index has pre-existing deletions or if the method is called multiple times.

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L118-L147)

## State Management and Reset

Both safelist and blocklist operations persist for the lifetime of the `CellAnnotation` instance, affecting all subsequent predictions. The system provides a reset mechanism to clear all filters and restore full access to the reference database.

```python
def reset_knn(self):
    """Reset the knn such that nothing is marked deleted."""
    self.blocklist = None
    self.safelist = None
    
    # HNSW does not track marked status, so we unmark all
    for i in self.idx2label:
        try:
            self.knn.unmark_deleted(i)
        except:
            pass  # Ignore if not marked
```

Calling `reset_knn()` clears both filter attributes and attempts to unmark all deleted indices in the HNSW index. The try-except pattern handles edge cases where indices may not be marked, ensuring robust operation across different index states.

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L74-L91)

## Practical Workflow

The typical workflow for applying safelist/blocklist filters involves three phases: discovery, selection, and annotation. The tutorial demonstrates this pattern using a lung tissue dataset, where the researcher first identifies available cell types, then selects a biologically relevant subset.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Initialize CellAnnotation] --> B[Discover Available Classes]
    B --> C[Select Filter Strategy]
    C --> D{Safelist or Blocklist?}
    D -->|Safelist| E[Define permitted types]
    D -->|Blocklist| F[Define excluded types]
    E --> G["Apply safelist_celltypes()"]
    F --> H["Apply blocklist_celltypes()"]
    G --> I[Run annotation]
    H --> I
    I --> J[Analyze results]
    J --> K{Need different filter?}
    K -->|Yes| L[reset_knn]
    L --> C
    K -->|No| M[Complete]
```

The `classes` property provides convenient access to all available cell type labels in the reference database, enabling informed filter selection based on domain knowledge.

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L68-L73)

## Practical Example: Lung Dataset Annotation

The cell annotation tutorial demonstrates safelist usage for analyzing lung scRNA-seq data from Adams et al., 2020. The researcher identifies lung-relevant cell types and applies a safelist to constrain predictions to biologically plausible annotations for this tissue context.

```python
# Discover available cell types
print("\n".join(ca.classes))

# Define lung-specific cell types
target_celltypes = [
    "lung macrophage",
    "alveolar macrophage",
    "classical monocyte",
    "non-classical monocyte",
    "conventional dendritic cell",
    "plasmacytoid dendritic cell",
    "CD4-positive, alpha-beta T cell",
    "regulatory T cell",
    "CD8-positive, alpha-beta T cell",
    "B cell",
    "plasma cell",
    "type I pneumocyte",
    "type II pneumocyte",
    "club cell",
    "lung ciliated cell",
    "basal cell",
    "endothelial cell of vascular tree",
    "fibroblast",
    "myofibroblast cell",
    # ... additional lung-specific types
]

# Apply safelist constraint
ca.safelist_celltypes(target_celltypes)

# Perform annotation with constrained search space
adams = ca.annotate_dataset(adams)
```

This approach eliminates biologically implausible annotations (such as "retinal bipolar neuron" or "keratinocyte") that might appear due to transcriptional similarities, ensuring results are biologically contextualized to lung tissue.

Sources: [cell_annotation_tutorial.ipynb](docs/notebooks/cell_annotation_tutorial.ipynb#L607-L681)

## API Reference

### safelist_celltypes

Explicitly permits only specified cell types to appear in annotation results. Mutually exclusive with blocklist.

```python
safelist_celltypes(labels: Union[List[str], Set[str]]) -> None
```

**Parameters:**
- `labels`: List or set of cell type labels to permit

**Behavior:**
- Clears any existing blocklist
- Marks all reference cells as deleted
- Unmarks cells belonging to specified labels
- Persists until changed or `reset_knn()` is called

**Example:**
```python
ca.safelist_celltypes(["T cell", "B cell", "macrophage"])
```

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L118-L147)

### blocklist_celltypes

Excludes specified cell types from annotation results. Mutually exclusive with safelist.

```python
blocklist_celltypes(labels: Union[List[str], Set[str]]) -> None
```

**Parameters:**
- `labels`: List or set of cell type labels to exclude

**Behavior:**
- Clears any existing safelist
- Marks cells belonging to specified labels as deleted
- Preserves access to all other cell types
- Persists until changed or `reset_knn()` is called

**Example:**
```python
ca.blocklist_celltypes(["unknown cell", "low quality cell"])
```

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L92-L117)

### reset_knn

Clears all safelist and blocklist filters, restoring full access to the reference database.

```python
reset_knn() -> None
```

**Behavior:**
- Sets `self.safelist = None`
- Sets `self.blocklist = None`
- Attempts to unmark all deleted indices in the kNN index

**Example:**
```python
ca.reset_knn()  # Clear all filters
```

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L74-L91)

### classes

Property that returns the set of all viable prediction cell type labels available in the reference.

```python
@property
classes -> set
```

**Returns:**
- Set of all cell type label strings from `label2int` keys

**Example:**
```python
available_types = ca.classes
print(f"Total available: {len(available_types)}")
print("Sample types:", list(available_types)[:5])
```

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L68-L73)

> [!TIP]
> The safelist operation marks all cells as deleted before unmarking permitted types, which can impact performance if safelisting a small subset of a large reference. For large-scale analyses where you need to annotate to a small subset of cell types repeatedly, consider creating a filtered kNN index rather than applying safelist at runtime.

## Comparison Table

| Feature | Safelist | Blocklist | No Filter |
|---------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| **Use Case** | Tissue-specific annotation | Removing low-quality/artifact types | Exploratory analysis |
| **Default State** | All excluded, then permitted types enabled | All enabled, then specified types excluded | All cell types enabled |
| **Performance** | Slower (marks all, then unmarks subset) | Faster (marks only subset) | Fastest (no marking) |
| **Semantics** | Inclusionary (white list) | Exclusionary (black list) | Unconstrained |
| **Best For** | Small number of relevant cell types | Few problematic cell types | Discovery and characterization |
| **Persistence** | Until changed or reset | Until changed or reset | N/A |

> [!TIP]
> Safelist and blocklist are mutually exclusive. Setting a safelist automatically clears the blocklist, and vice versa. This design prevents ambiguous filter states where a cell type might be both included and excluded.

## Integration with Annotation Pipeline

The safelist/blocklist filters integrate seamlessly with the two primary annotation methods in `CellAnnotation`:

```python
# Method 1: Using annotate_dataset (high-level, automatic embedding)
ca.safelist_celltypes(["T cell", "B cell", "macrophage"])
annotated_data = ca.annotate_dataset(data)
# Results constrained to safelisted types in data.obs["celltype_hint"]

# Method 2: Using get_predictions_knn (detailed control with stats)
ca.blocklist_celltypes(["unknown cell", "low quality cell"])
predictions, nn_idxs, nn_dists, stats = ca.get_predictions_knn(
    embeddings, 
    k=50, 
    weighting=True
)
# Results exclude blocklisted types, stats include full query metrics
```

Both methods respect the active filter state at the time of invocation, allowing dynamic filter application throughout an analysis workflow. The `annotate_dataset` method provides a streamlined interface that computes embeddings automatically, while `get_predictions_knn` offers granular control over kNN search parameters and returns detailed statistics for each prediction.

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L148-L280), [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L281-L320)

## Next Steps

Having understood safelist and blocklist mechanisms, you may want to explore:

- **[Understanding Cell Type Classification](14-understanding-cell-type-classification)**: Learn about the underlying classification algorithms and consensus mechanisms that generate predictions
- **[Prediction Weighting Strategies](16-prediction-weighting-strategies)**: Understand how distance-based weighting affects consensus predictions and confidence metrics
- **[Cell Annotation API Reference](13-cell-annotation-api-reference)**: Complete API documentation for all annotation methods and parameters

The combination of precise filter control with robust classification algorithms enables sophisticated, biologically contextualized cell type annotation across diverse tissue types and experimental conditions.

# Prediction Weighting Strategies



This page explores SCimilarity's prediction weighting mechanisms that enhance cell type annotation accuracy and confidence assessment through distance-aware voting, loss balancing during model training, and statistical confidence metrics. These strategies enable more nuanced predictions by leveraging proximity information in the embedding space and balancing different loss components during training.

## Distance-Weighted kNN Classification

The core prediction weighting strategy in SCimilarity operates within the k-nearest neighbors voting mechanism during cell type annotation. When enabled, this approach weights each neighbor's vote inversely proportional to its distance from the query cell, giving greater influence to closer and thus more similar reference cells.

**Implementation Mechanics**: The `get_predictions_knn` method in the `CellAnnotation` class accepts a `weighting` parameter that toggles this behavior. When `weighting=True`, each neighbor contributes `1.0 / max(distance, 1e-6)` to its corresponding cell type's accumulated score rather than a uniform vote count of 1.0. This mathematical formulation ensures that closer neighbors have exponentially higher influence while maintaining numerical stability with the epsilon guard term.

**Distance Calculation Flow**:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Query Cell Embedding] --> B[HNSW kNN Search<br/>Retrieve k=50 neighbors]
    B --> C{Weighting Mode?}
    C -->|Disabled| D[Uniform Voting<br/>Each neighbor = +1.0 vote]
    C -->|Enabled| E[Distance-Weighted Voting<br/>Each neighbor = 1.0 / max dist, 1e-6]
    D --> F[Accumulate Votes by Cell Type]
    E --> F
    F --> G[Predict Cell Type<br/>Max accumulated score]
    G --> H[Compute Confidence Metrics<br/>vs2nd, vsAll, weighted variants]
```

The distance weighting provides two key advantages: it reduces noise from borderline neighbors and improves precision when the embedding space has well-defined cell type boundaries with varying degrees of overlap.

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L148-L279)

## Weighted Confidence Metrics

SCimilarity computes comprehensive confidence statistics that distinguish between simple vote-based confidence and distance-weighted confidence, enabling users to assess prediction reliability through multiple lenses.

**Metrics Overview**:

| Metric | Description | Weighting Variant |
|--------|-------------|-------------------|
| `hits` | JSON string with vote counts per cell type | `hits_weighted` |
| `vs2nd` | Ratio of top cell type to second best | `vs2nd_weighted` |
| `vsAll` | Ratio of top cell type to total votes | `vsAll_weighted` |
| `min_dist` / `max_dist` | Distance range to nearest neighbors | — |

**Confidence Calculation Pattern**: For weighted metrics, the system first converts raw accumulated weights to comparable values by applying `max(weight, 1e-6)` to ensure non-zero denominators. The `vs2nd_weighted` metric divides the top-weighted cell type score by the sum of top and second-best scores, providing a value between 0.5 (ambiguous) and 1.0 (highly confident). Similarly, `vsAll_weighted` compares the top score to all summed weights, indicating dominance.

These metrics enable downstream filtering and quality control, allowing users to set thresholds on confidence scores and separate high-confidence predictions from uncertain classifications that may require manual review.

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L215-L273)

## Training Loss Weighting

During model training, SCimilarity employs a weighted loss combination that balances triplet loss (which enforces metric learning constraints) against reconstruction loss (which preserves gene expression information through the decoder). This weighting is critical for achieving both discriminative latent representations and faithful reconstruction capabilities.

**Mixed Loss Architecture**:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Input Cells] --> B[Encoder Network]
    B --> C[Latent Embeddings]
    C --> D[Decoder Network]
    D --> E[Reconstructed Cells]
    C --> F[Triplet Loss Function<br/>Metric Learning]
    E --> G[MSE Loss Function<br/>Reconstruction]
    F --> H[Mixed Loss Calculation<br/>w₁·Triplet + w₂·MSE]
    G --> H
    H --> I[Backpropagation<br/>Model Update]
```

**Weight Parameter Configuration**: The `triplet_loss_weight` parameter (default: 0.001) controls the balance between the two loss components through the formula: `total_loss = (triplet_loss_weight × triplet_loss) + ((1.0 - triplet_loss_weight) × mse)`. Extreme values (0 or 1) produce pure reconstruction or pure metric learning models respectively, while intermediate values enable joint optimization.

The default heavily favors reconstruction, reflecting SCimilarity's design priority of maintaining gene expression interpretability while still learning meaningful distance metrics. Users may increase this weight for applications requiring stricter metric separation at the cost of reconstruction fidelity.

Sources: [training_models.py](src/scimilarity/training_models.py#L73-L93), [training_models.py](src/scimilarity/training_models.py#L293-L315)

## Practical Application Patterns

The choice of weighting strategy depends on data characteristics and analysis goals. Understanding when to employ each approach enables optimal annotation quality.

**Distance Weighting Decision Matrix**:

| Data Characteristic | Recommended Weighting | Rationale |
|---------------------|----------------------|-----------|
| Clear cell type clusters | Unweighted (default) | Simple majority voting sufficient |
| Overlapping cell type boundaries | Weighted (`weighting=True`) | Closer neighbors more discriminative |
| Sparse reference coverage | Weighted | Limited neighbors need emphasis |
| High-dimensional noise | Weighted | Distance weighting reduces outlier influence |
| Computational efficiency critical | Unweighted | Slightly faster without reciprocal calculations |

**Statistical Thresholding Pattern**: Use confidence metrics to filter predictions and create high-confidence annotation subsets. For example, filter cells where `vs2nd_weighted > 0.8` to retain only predictions with strong dominance over the second-best alternative, or use `vsAll_weighted` to ensure predictions account for a substantial proportion of weighted votes across all k neighbors.

**Tutorial Example**: The cell annotation tutorial demonstrates using `weighting=True` when calling `get_predictions_knn` on lung scRNA-seq data, showing how this parameter improves prediction coherence in heterogeneous tissue contexts where cell type boundaries may be less distinct.

Sources: [cell_annotation_tutorial.ipynb](docs/notebooks/cell_annotation_tutorial.ipynb#L330-L334)

## Advanced Configuration Strategies

For researchers requiring fine-grained control over prediction behavior, SCimilarity offers several advanced weighting configuration options that can be combined for specialized use cases.

**Custom Weighting Combinations**: Users can compute multiple prediction variants (weighted and unweighted) simultaneously and compare confidence metrics to identify cells where weighting significantly alters predictions—these often represent biologically interesting boundary cases or transitional states.

**Confidence Metric Integration**: Combine multiple confidence metrics in custom scoring schemes. For example, require both `vs2nd_weighted > 0.7` and `vsAll_weighted > 0.5` to ensure predictions are both dominant relative to the runner-up and represent a meaningful proportion of total neighborhood weight.

> [!TIP]
> When working with novel cell types not present in the reference, examine low-confidence predictions across all metrics—these may represent previously uncharacterized cell states or artifacts requiring further investigation.

**Loss Weight Optimization**: Experiment with `triplet_loss_weight` during model training for domain-specific applications. Increase this value for applications prioritizing cell type separation (e.g., classification tasks) or decrease it for applications requiring accurate gene expression reconstruction (e.g., differential expression analysis from embeddings).

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L234-L273), [training_models.py](src/scimilarity/training_models.py#L309-L314)

## Implementation Considerations

When deploying weighting strategies in production pipelines or large-scale analyses, several implementation factors influence performance and interpretability.

**Computational Overhead**: Distance weighting introduces minimal computational cost—a single reciprocal operation per neighbor. For large datasets with millions of cells, this remains negligible compared to the kNN search itself (dominated by HNSW index operations).

**Numerical Stability**: The epsilon term `1e-6` in distance weighting prevents division by zero and ensures well-defined behavior when query cells exactly match reference embeddings (distance = 0). This guard also provides a maximum weight cap, preventing any single neighbor from having infinite influence.

**Metric Consistency**: Weighted and unweighted metrics are computed simultaneously within the same loop, ensuring they reflect identical neighbor selections and distance measurements. This design enables direct comparison without re-running kNN searches.

> [!TIP]
> The `reset_knn` method allows clearing deletion marks applied by safelist/blocklist operations without reloading the reference, enabling efficient iterative refinement of annotation queries with different cell type constraints.

Sources: [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L237-L239), [cell_annotation.py](src/scimilarity/cell_annotation.py#L74-L80)

- Review [Understanding Cell Type Classification](14-understanding-cell-type-classification) for the complete annotation workflow
- Explore [Safelist and Blocklist Cell Types](15-safelist-and-blocklist-cell-types) for constraint-based annotation control
- Reference [Cell Annotation API Reference](13-cell-annotation-api-reference) for detailed method documentation
